gap: No result ChatGPT got states, for a named extender, what its 'one-cable' claim needs: the Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro runs both added screens over one cable only with a DisplayLink-style driver, needs two DisplayPort-enabled USB-C ports to skip the driver, and on a plain M1/M2 MacBook (or the MacBook Neo) drives just one screen without that software. The single-screen Duex Float 2 Pro runs over one USB-C cable with no driver.
standout_why: I read itechguides' 2026 list and its cited 2025 list (both cited by ChatGPT), plus The Office Journal's and WorkCocoon's 16-inch pages (top results). The itechguides pages give general warnings: 'one USB-C cable does not mean one cable works with every laptop', DisplayLink 'may require drivers', and 'MacBook compatibility cannot be reduced to yes or no'. The 2025 page also lists the Trio 3 Pro as 'single USB-C cable setup' without saying a driver is needed. They name the driver-or-port condition only for no-name Amazon listings (ZUMWALT, KYY). The Office Journal and WorkCocoon cover only no-name 16-inch portable monitors and do not mention drivers or MacBook display limits. ChatGPT's own answer has the general caution ('some extenders require DisplayLink drivers', 'particularly some MacBooks') but does not tie it to any product, and it recommends Flexpire for 'single-cable USB-C setup' without saying what that needs. So rivals have the general idea, but none has a per-product table of video paths.
decides: This confirms the Duex Float 2 Pro as the safe pick for a 16-inch laptop of unknown make. It adds one screen over a single USB-C cable with no driver, and one added screen stays within the one-external-display limit of plain M-chip MacBooks (the limit is per Macworld). The Trio 3 Pro, and probably the three-panel FOPO S788 (driver required per our records), win only for shoppers who accept a DisplayLink-style driver or whose laptop has two DP-enabled USB-C ports and drives two external displays (M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max, any M4/M5 per Macworld). This also flips ChatGPT's 'single-cable' framing of triple-screen rigs: on these models, one cable usually means a driver.

findings.label: Driver-free condition
findings.value: Two DP-enabled USB-C ports on the laptop (one cable per screen, no driver); otherwise a software driver Macworld likens to DisplayLink
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review: MacBook's dual QHD screen wingspan (Simon Jary, Macworld, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Macworld quotes the manual: 'if your laptop has two DP enabled USB-C ports … driver installation is not necessary.' Ships with two USB-C cables (20 in / 0.5 m).

findings.label: MacBooks that run both screens without the software
findings.value: M1/M2/M3 Pro or Max, and any M4/M5 MacBook; plain M1 and M2 and the MacBook Neo connect only one monitor without the software
findings.note: Macworld's wording. Elsewhere it says Macs 'as or more powerful than a standard M1/M2/M3' need no download, which conflicts with the M1/M2 limit. The page should follow the specific limit.

findings.label: Fit range and brightness
findings.note: Tested on a 14-inch MacBook Pro, not a 16-inch. Full brightness needs a power adapter on one Trio USB-C port, which passes through up to 65 W.

findings.label: Video path
findings.value: One USB-C cable carries video, data and up to 65 W pass-through; 'no drivers or software to install on either Windows or macOS'; mini HDMI fallback for laptops without USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode, needing a separate power source
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro Review (James Smythe, Mighty Gadget, 2026-08-16, updated 2026-08-20)
findings.note: Tested on an Honor Windows laptop. The review doesn't say which connection gives 120 Hz. One added screen fits within the one-external-display limit Macworld gives for plain M1/M2 MacBooks (my inference from the two sources).
